newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria protests ease pressure on troubled banks.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria protests ease pressure on troubled banks.

text.p: Ten days of street protests against the ruling Socialists and in support of opposition demands for early elections have eased pressure on ailing Bulgarian banks from anxious depositors, a banker said.

"It is a paradox, but now no one draws money from banks because people have transferred the tension of discontent with those in power away from banks and onto the streets," said a senior local commercial banker, who declined to be named.

The ex-communist Socialist party's opponents have organised the protests on the back of public anger over deepening economic hardship. Workers held a series of one-hour warning strikes around the country on Wednesday.

Falling confidence in the national currency and economy escalated into a massive withdrawal of deposits. Around one billion dollars in personal savings have been withdrawn from local banks in the past year.
One quarter of Bulgaria's 40-odd commercial banks were placed in receivership last year. Savings and company deposits in nine banks are frozen until courts rule on their solvency.

Several bank stabilisation programmes agreed with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have been launched in recent years but none completed, and banks are suffering severe liquidity crises.

The Bank Consolidation Company (BCC), set up five years ago to merge into larger institutions scores of local banks and then privatise them, said that yet another stabilisation programme would be postponed this year because of the unrest.
"Without political stability and an agreement with the IMF, it will be impossible to sell banks," BCC director Valentin Tsvetanov told Reuters.
The IMF has said it is prepared to complete talks on a reform and funding agreement to haul Bulgaria's crumbling economy back from the brink of default as soon as a stable government is in place.

The Fund had begun talks with the outgoing Socialist government, which resigned on December 21, on the implementation of a strict fixed exchange rate regime as a last resort to restore confidence in the financial system.
The Socialists appeared on Wednesday to soften their stand on opposition calls for a general election and suggested an early poll before the end of this year. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
